title.analysis: 'Why Everything Changes After You Lose Your Job In 2026' reuses the channel's 'Why Everything Changes After X' template, but swaps the usual aspirational milestone (a dollar threshold, a paid-off asset) for a negative life event. In this channel the template performs best when X is a concrete, desirable financial milestone: 2DBQnxaDScs 'Why Everything Changes After Paying Off Your House' 18.82947x STRONG and vXBhBlBIUDs '... After Paying Off Your Car Loan' 3.43336x STRONG. It is weaker when X is a modest or ambiguous level: rbnPR2Dnmz4 '... After $50,000 A Year' 0.27802x WEAK and _ArhEBNhT_8 '... After $100,000 Per Year' 0.60981x TYPICAL. The closest topic sibling, _6Zvfj0ThsQ 'Why Stable Jobs Are Financially Riskier Than Ever In 2026' 1.0174x TYPICAL, framed job insecurity as a warning to employed viewers rather than an event that has already happened to them. Brutal-2026 household titles land in between: 4pnSNmGTGkk 'Why "Normal" People Are Going Broke in 2026' 1.43818x TYPICAL versus nYcSSd5V5_4 'The Shocking Cost of Being Normal in 2026' 0.4849x WEAK; R_E6OOnF9e4 '15 Low Effort Boring Tasks That Make More Than Your Job' 0.59678x TYPICAL. Interpretation: the title contains no number, no dollar figure and no named mechanism (UI, COBRA, AI), and it addresses only viewers who have lost a job or fear it, while the template's aspirational promise ('everything changes' as reward) is inverted into a threat. This is a descriptive pattern over eight titles, not a proven cause.
title.search_demand: Moderate explicit intent exists for 'lost my job what to do', 'unemployment benefits', 'COBRA cost'; this title does not contain those query terms, so it relies on browse/suggested distribution. Historical query volume and traffic sources unavailable.
title.script_alignment: Strongly aligned on 'lose your job' and '2026' (the script is built around 2026 conditions: ACA subsidy expiry, JOLTS hiring rate, AI displacement). 'Everything changes' is paid off by the thesis that job loss is 'structurally different' now, but most of the runtime explains what changed in the economy and safety net rather than what changes for the viewer personally after loss; the personal-action payoff is only a short savings-account coda.

thumbnail.analysis: Registered maxresdefault fetched fresh and inspected at native 1280x720 and proportional 320x180. White background. Left third: a cartoon man with orange-red hair, wide round eyes, open shocked mouth, both hands pressed to his cheeks, grey T-shirt; a classic panic pose. Top right: very large black condensed uppercase text 'IT'S' on one line and 'HAPPENING...' below with an ellipsis. Below the text: a hand-drawn line chart with the y-axis labelled 'JOB OPENINGS' and the x-axis 'TIME', a thick red line that rises briefly then falls in steps to a red downward arrow at the right; inside the plot nine small dark worker silhouettes (some with hard hats) each struck through with a red X. A thick black curved arrow from the upper right points down at the falling end of the line. Hierarchy: text first, face second, chart third. At 320px the text 'IT'S HAPPENING...' remains clearly legible and the face reads as shock; the falling red line and the red X marks still read as 'fewer jobs', but the axis labels 'JOB OPENINGS' and 'TIME' become small and hard to read. The image is about the labour market (falling job openings) and a vague 'it's happening' alarm, while the title is about personal job loss; neither the image nor the title shows money, insurance or the Keon story. 'IT'S HAPPENING...' is a generic alarm phrase that does not name what is happening, so the chart carries the entire meaning; the script does cite openings falling from 12 million to 6.9 million, so the chart is supported by the transcript in direction (the drawn curve is illustrative, not data). Historical continuity, A/B testing and CTR contribution are unverified.

script.opening_words: It's 9:47 on a Tuesday morning in March and Keon is on a Zoom call he's barely listening to.
script.ending_words: And if you haven't subscribed yet, now's the time because Keon's story is not over, and neither is yours.
script.analysis: Full 16,359 canonical characters read in two contiguous chunks (0-10,000, 10,000-16,359). The hook is the strongest writing in the video: a minute-by-minute cold open (9:47, 10:00, 10:02, 10:14, 10:17, 10:30) with tactile objects (cardboard box, coffee mug, kids' photo, unread severance envelope) that makes the layoff feel real before any statistic appears. 'My name is Nick and here's what that envelope doesn't tell him' turns the envelope into a curiosity device. The whole video is then structured as a single-character case study (Keon, 38, $140,000, Dallas suburb), and each statistical section is anchored back to him ('This is the market Keon just walked into', 'Keon is in Texas, so his max is $560'), which is an effective technique for turning a dense statistics list into a narrative. Transitions work through escalation of personal stakes: unemployment rate, then search, then UI, then 'the moment that breaks him comes two days later' (health insurance), then the household budget, then the 401(k) temptation, then mental health. The 'moment that breaks him' line is a well-placed pattern interrupt that resets attention at about 6,000 characters. Weak points: (1) the statistical density is extreme, with roughly 50 numbers stated, many unsourced, and the AI/ghost-job section reads as a list rather than story; (2) the declared thesis arrives late ('I need you to pay attention to the next part because this is the thesis of the entire video' at about 10,850 of 16,359 characters) and it is a policy argument about the expiring safety net, which pivots away from the personal finance promised by the title; (3) the 'one I've been hinting at this entire video' AI callback is a good open-loop payoff (it ties back to the 43 filtered applications), but stacking a third macro theme after the thesis makes the back half feel like a series of essays; (4) the recap introduces a new number ('the $500 median emergency fund') that was never established; (5) the actionable payoff is a single paragraph (open a high-yield savings account, $200 plus $400 every two weeks), so a viewer in Keon's situation gets almost no practical guidance on UI filing, COBRA versus marketplace special enrollment, severance negotiation or 401(k) alternatives. The 'door' metaphor and the 9:47 Tuesday callback close the loop elegantly. Factual reliability is mixed: several figures reproduce reputable sources (KFF $888 to $1,904; KFF family premium x 102% for COBRA; BLS hires 3.1%), but the script applies a Texas state income tax that does not exist and understates the Texas UI maximum. All stored text read; not an original-audio, editing or retention verification.

beat_map.beat: Cold-open micro-timeline: 9:47 Zoom call, 10:00 'quick sync' invite with director and HR, 10:02 meeting, 10:14 logged out, 10:17 badge dead, 10:30 in the car with a cardboard box, kids' photo and unread severance envelope

Nick intro ('here's what that envelope doesn't tell him'), 'the version of job loss his dad lived through, it's gone' thesis tease, promise to track Keon's money, health insurance and timeline, like request

Character setup: Keon 38, software engineer, $140,000; wife Yana part-time nurse because childcare equals her old salary; Dallas-suburb house, $3,200 mortgage, $9,000 savings 'less than two months of their actual expenses'

Labour-market statistics: 4.3% unemployment compared with March 2018; hiring rate 3.1% 'tied with April 2020'; 'low hire low fire' (ASR: 'low higher low fire'); openings 12 million to 6.9 million versus 7.6 million unemployed

Keon's search: 78 applications, three replies by week five; 15 to 42 to about 100 applications per interview; LinkedIn $125,000-plus hiring down 32%; 25.7-week average search; 43 of 78 screened by AI filters
Ghost jobs: one in five listings; 93% of HR professionals admit posting them

Unemployment insurance as a state lottery: Washington $1,152 versus Mississippi $235; Texas max $560 versus $2,700 weekly pay (about 20%); benefits taxable via 1099-G; 12-week states; Missouri 8-to-20-week indexing

Health-coverage shock: enhanced ACA subsidies expired December 31, 2025; $888 to $1,904 (114%); 400% FPL cliff; $2,180 per month benchmark family quote ($26,160 per year); COBRA 102% rule, $2,294 per month / $27,533 per year, 'a new Toyota Corolla every year'

Household runway math: eight weeks severance $21,500 gross to about $14,000 net; UI $2,240 per month to about $1,900; $7,800 burn versus $3,800 income; $4,000 monthly deficit; severance 3.5 months plus savings 2 months equals six, matched to the average search length

401(k) temptation: $185,000 balance; 6% of participants took hardship withdrawals in 2025, triple pre-pandemic; $25,000 withdrawal nets about $15,000; $25,000 at 7% for 25 years about $136,000, 'real cost closer to $120,000'

Psychological cost: depression treatment rates, one in five clinically depressed after six months, 70% higher suicide risk, Harvard 33% divorce figure, children 15% more likely held back; Marienthal study's five latent functions of work; Keon's sleep, avoidance and dishwasher argument

Stated thesis: 2008 $787 billion stimulus and 2020 pandemic programmes (extra $600 then $300 a week, PUA, $3,600 child tax credit, moratoria) contrasted with 2026 expirations (ACA subsidies, SAVE plan, Medicaid unwinding 25 million, SNAP $186 billion, gig workers without federal UI); 'allowed to expire program by program'

AI variable callback to the 43 filtered applications: Stanford August 2025 payroll study (minus 13% for ages 22 to 25 in AI-exposed jobs, 20% for young developers), Salesforce 9,000 to 5,000, Microsoft $500 million call-centre savings, Snap 40% AI code, Amazon 30,000 corporate cuts, Anthropic CEO 50% entry-level warning; Keon's old team replacing three analyst roles

Recap montage: frozen hiring, six-month search, UI lottery, health cliff, '$500 median emergency fund' (first appearance), expired safety net, AI; 'not just financially harder, it's structurally different'
Resolution: re-employed at eight months at $118,000 ($22,000 less); wage-scarring claim; 'roughly half a million dollars in future wealth'
Action and moral: high-yield savings account, $200 start, $400 every two weeks; 'a door he can close behind him'; callback to 9:47 Tuesday; 'the ones who built the door before they needed it'
Close: 'rules of job loss have changed, rules of preparation haven't'; comment prompt ('which part hit hardest') and subscribe ask framed as 'Keon's story is not over'

claim_audit: 'Keon is in Texas, so his max is $560 a week': UNDERSTATED. Secondary pages citing the Texas Workforce Commission benefit table give a maximum of $605 per week effective October 5, 2025, in force at publication (2026-04-25); $560 to $577 match earlier years. TWC page itself was not opened, so treat $605 as secondary-sourced. The narrator's '$2,700 a week' is consistent with $140,000 / 52 = $2,692, and $560 / $2,700 = 20.7% (analyst calculation); at $605 the replacement is about 22.4%. '$560 a week or about $2,240 a month' uses four weeks; a calendar month averages 4.33 weeks, so $560 x 52 / 12 = $2,427 (analyst calculation).

'Texas state tax' on severance and 'federal, state, and penalty' on the 401(k) withdrawal: ERROR. Texas levies no personal income tax, which the script itself sets up by placing Keon outside Dallas. Severance math: $140,000 / 52 x 8 = $21,538 gross (matches $21,500); 22% supplemental federal withholding plus 7.65% FICA leaves about $15,125, not 'around $14,000' (analyst calculation; FICA wage-base and actual year-end liability ignored). 401(k): $25,000 less 22% federal and 10% penalty nets about $17,000 (about $16,500 at 24%), not 'maybe $15,000'; the '$10,000 to access his own money' is therefore overstated by roughly $1,500 to $2,000 for a Texas resident, and a year of reduced income could put him in a lower bracket. Also, after separation from the employer this is an ordinary distribution, not technically a 'hardship withdrawal' (narrator conflates the two).

'$25,000 ... at a 7% average return over the next 25 years, would have grown to roughly $136,000 ... the real cost ... closer to $120,000': $25,000 x 1.07^25 = $135,686, correct (analyst calculation). The $120,000 figure subtracts today's $15,000 net cash from a future nominal value, mixing present and future dollars; the forgone future value is about $136,000, and its present-value cost is the $25,000 itself plus taxes. Rhetorically effective but methodologically muddled.

'The average annual payment jumped from $888 to $1,904. A 114% increase overnight': matches KFF's issue brief (published 2025, before the video), $1,904 / $888 - 1 = 114.4% (analyst calculation). But KFF's figure is a projection of net premium payments for subsidized enrollees, not observed 'premiums', and the narrator states it as realized fact ('on January 1st, premiums more than doubled'). '22 million Americans' for enhanced-subsidy recipients is consistent with KFF's framing; not independently opened.

'The average Cobra premium for a family plan in 2026 is $2,294 a month. That's $27,533 a year': KFF 2025 Employer Health Benefits Survey average family premium is $26,993; $26,993 x 1.02 = $27,532.86 per year, $2,294.40 per month (analyst calculation), so the number reproduces exactly but it is the 2025 survey average, not a 2026 figure, and the narrator's monthly x 12 is $27,528 (rounding only). The 102% COBRA cap is correct (DOL rule).

'Hiring has collapsed to 3.1%, which is tied with April 2020 for the lowest rate on record' and 'Job openings ... down to 6.9 million ... 7.6 million unemployed': BLS JOLTS shows a February 2026 hires rate of 3.1% and openings of about 6.9 million (March 2026 release of May 5, 2026, after publication, shows hires back up to 3.5% and openings 6.866 million). The 3.1% figure was the latest available at publication; the 'tied with April 2020 for the lowest on record' qualifier and the 7.6 million unemployed figure were not verified (UNVERIFIED). '4.3% ... roughly where unemployment sat in March 2018': BLS March 2018 rate was about 4.0% from analyst recollection, not re-fetched; treat comparison as approximate/UNVERIFIED. The 12 million 2022 openings peak is consistent with JOLTS (about 12.1 million, March 2022), not re-fetched.

'6% of 401k participants took a hardship withdrawal in 2025. That's triple the pre-pandemic rate': Vanguard How America Saves 2026 reports 6% of participants permitted to take hardship withdrawals initiated one in 2025 (up from about 5% in 2024). The full HAS 2026 report was released around June 2026, after publication; whether the 6% figure was public by April 25, 2026 was not confirmed. 'Triple the pre-pandemic rate' (about 2%) is plausible but not verified against a specific pre-2020 edition. Note the denominator is participants in plans permitting hardship withdrawals, not all 401(k) participants.

'In 12 states, you don't even get the standard 26 weeks. Florida, North Carolina, Arkansas, Louisiana, and Tennessee cap benefits at 12 weeks': several of these states use sliding scales with 12 weeks as the minimum at low unemployment (e.g. Florida 12 to 23, North Carolina 12 to 20) rather than a flat cap; the state count of 12 and the Missouri 8-to-20-week law were not verified against DOL comparison tables (UNVERIFIED). 'Washington $1,152 ... Mississippi $235': Mississippi $235 is the long-standing maximum; Washington's figure not verified for the 2026 benefit year. Ratio $1,152 / $235 = 4.9 ('five times' correct as arithmetic).

Budget runway: $14,000 / $4,000 = 3.5 months and $9,000 / $4,000 = 2.25 months, about 5.75 months total, consistent with 'six months' (analyst calculation). The $7,800 burn includes $2,294 COBRA, so the earlier claim that $9,000 is 'less than two months of their actual expenses' is internally consistent ($9,000 / $7,800 = 1.15 months). '25.7 weeks' average duration of unemployment was not re-fetched from BLS (UNVERIFIED for the exact value).

'That gap, compounded over 25 years of retirement contributions, is roughly half a million dollars in future wealth': no derivation given. A $22,000 annual gap uncompounded over 25 years is $550,000 (salary, not retirement contributions); contributing 10% of the gap at 7% for 25 years gives about $139,000 (analyst calculation). The 'half a million' figure is therefore unclear in method and likely overstated if it refers to retirement contributions.

Other statistics stated without source and not checked here (UNVERIFIED): 100 applications per interview, LinkedIn 32% decline in $125,000-plus hiring, 43 of 78 applications screened by AI (presented as a fact about a fictional character), one in five listings ghost jobs, 93% of HR professionals posting ghost jobs, one in three laid-off workers receiving severance, 70% higher suicide risk, $500 median emergency fund (introduced only in the recap). Broadly consistent with known public reports but not opened: Stanford 'Canaries in the Coal Mine' August 2025 (13% relative decline ages 22 to 25), Salesforce 9,000 to 5,000 and 'I need less heads', Microsoft $500 million call-centre savings, Amazon about 30,000 corporate cuts, Anthropic CEO 50% entry-level warning, Medicaid unwinding about 25 million disenrollments, CBO SNAP $186 billion, Marienthal study's five latent functions, Killewald (Harvard) 33% divorce finding.

'In 2008 ... Washington deployed a $787 billion dollar stimulus': the $787 billion American Recovery and Reinvestment Act was signed in February 2009 (2008's stimulus was the smaller Economic Stimulus Act rebates); date imprecise. 'The safety net wasn't destroyed. Nobody voted to destroy it' conflicts with the script's own SNAP '$186 billion' cut and the SAVE plan ending, which were legislative or administrative decisions; this is narrator opinion.

Possible ASR artefacts preserved, not corrected against audio: 'low higher low fire equilibrium' (likely 'low hire, low fire'), 'sounds like a a normal economy', 'before human read them', 'save student loan plan' (likely 'SAVE'), 'more than $5 trillion stimulus checks' (phrase likely truncated), '$787 billion dollar'.

topic.analysis: Job loss in a 2026 low-hire labour market: household runway, unemployment insurance, health coverage after the ACA enhanced-subsidy expiry, retirement-account raids, mental-health cost, safety-net rollback and AI displacement of entry-level white-collar work. Timely (tied to 2025-2026 policy and labour-market data); audience is employed mid-career workers anxious about layoffs plus recently laid-off viewers. Distinctive audience question: 'What actually happens to my money if I get laid off this year?' The script answers the diagnosis well but offers little prescriptive guidance.
topic.novelty_and_corpus_angle: Original opportunity: a practical 'first 30 days after a layoff' sequence with verified numbers: file for UI immediately and check the state's actual maximum and duration (Texas $605 cap at the time, no state income tax), compare COBRA (102% of the employer premium, KFF family average $26,993 for 2025) against a marketplace plan via the job-loss special enrollment period, check whether severance delays UI eligibility in the viewer's state, and model the net cost of a 401(k) withdrawal correctly by state. Keep the Keon narrative device, which is the video's strongest asset, but correct the state-tax errors and label projections as projections.

virality.analysis: Observed result: 9,498 frozen views at 138.5741 days; ten-peer ratio 0.40294x WEAK and five-peer ratio 0.34283x WEAK, both independently reproduced, so the tier is robust across peer windows (the ten-peer ratio is near the 0.5 boundary). Likes 320 (3.37% of views) and comments 102 (1.07%) (channel baseline not computed), consistent with the explicit 'which part hit hardest' prompt and an emotionally personal topic. Evidence-backed interpretation: among its ten age peers, the STRONG videos are aspirational or self-comparison titles (compound interest levels 2.03193x, average 45-year-old 6.34409x, secretly wealthy 5.60724x); the same 'Why Everything Changes After' template published three to five days earlier with positive milestones ($500,000 invested 1.54694x, $100,000 per year 0.60981x) did better; this negative-event variant is the lowest of the template peers. Hypotheses: (a) the template's appeal relies on aspirational self-location ('have I reached X?'), which a job-loss event inverts into a threat that fewer viewers want to click; (b) the thumbnail's generic 'IT'S HAPPENING...' does not name the threat or a dollar stake; (c) the topic serves a narrower affected audience than milestone topics. Proposed experiment: in owned uploads, test the same Keon script under a concrete-stakes title (for example 'What Losing a $140K Job Actually Costs in 2026') and a thumbnail showing the COBRA or UI dollar figure, against a generic alarm thumbnail, measuring CTR, impressions and retention at the health-insurance and thesis transitions. None of these hypotheses is measurable here without impressions, CTR, traffic sources or retention.

alternative_explanations: Packaging hypothesis: negative-event framing and a generic 'IT'S HAPPENING...' thumbnail may lower click intent compared with aspirational milestones; CTR and impressions unavailable.
Audience-fit hypothesis: the channel's audience may skew toward investors tracking milestones, for whom job-loss content is less relevant; audience data unavailable.
Engagement hypothesis: a 1.07% comment rate suggests clicked viewers engaged strongly; retention unavailable.
Confounders: daily upload cadence with nearby STRONG peers competing for the same audience, algorithmic exploration timing, unknown later title or thumbnail edits.

original_content_lesson.test: Produce a verified 'layoff survival math' video keeping the minute-by-minute cold open and single-household case study, with state-correct taxes and UI maximums and COBRA versus marketplace comparison; test concrete dollar-stakes packaging versus generic alarm packaging in owned experiments, and measure CTR and retention at the thesis transition.
original_content_lesson.confidence: HIGH for the Texas state-tax error, severance/401(k) arithmetic and the KFF COBRA/ACA reproductions; MEDIUM for the Texas UI maximum (secondary sources) and the aspirational-versus-negative template pattern; LOW for causal virality attribution.
